findings.title: `organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the requester is not an organization member (e.g. org auth token / integration token auth, or a staff/superuser request that resolves no membership). Because `request.user.is_superuser` is `False` for non-user auth (and `AnonymousUser`), the second operand is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a 500 for those auth paths. The flag should only be computed inside the `optimized_pagination` branch and must null-check `member`.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is numeric-keyed but is used with the `datetime` column
findings.body: The endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and whose `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor integer. `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and a cursor value would be compared against a timestamp column as a bare integer in the generated `WHERE` clause. Any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an authorized user will therefore fail with a 500 instead of returning a page. Date-keyed querysets require `DateTimePaginator`-style key handling (the `multiplier` conversion).

findings.title: Negative slice start on a Django QuerySet raises ValueError, not "handled automatically"
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django explicitly rejects this: `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. Since `Cursor.from_string` happily parses a negative offset from the user-supplied `cursor` query parameter, a request like `?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-5:0` produces an unhandled exception / 500 rather than a 400. The inline comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` like `OffsetPaginator` does.

findings.title: BasePaginator now silently clamps negative cursor offsets, producing inconsistent cursors
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the behavior of every paginator derived from `BasePaginator` (issues, audit logs, many list endpoints). Previously a negative offset in a client-supplied cursor surfaced as an error from the ORM; now the query silently starts at row 0 while `build_cursor` is still handed the original negative `cursor.offset`. `_build_next_values` then computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the negative value and `_build_prev_values` treats the negative offset as "has_prev", so the returned next/prev cursors point at positions that do not correspond to the rows actually returned, causing skipped or duplicated rows on subsequent pages. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly rather than clamped.

findings.title: Prev-page trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice start
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the extra-row trim condition `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` uses the raw `cursor.offset`, while the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which may differ, e.g. clamped to 0 or negative). When `offset` is negative the comparison can never be true (or is true for the wrong row count), so the extra look-behind row fetched for `is_prev` cursors is not dropped and leaks into the returned page, duplicating a row the client already saw. The condition should compare against `start_offset + limit + extra`.

findings.title: Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
findings.body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced 10x reduction in the maximum redirect-chain depth: traces whose parent/child redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to the correct `set_key`, so their spans get split across multiple segments and are emitted as separate (incorrect) segments. If the reduction is intentional it should be stated in the PR and the caveat comment kept; otherwise the original bound should be restored.

findings.title: Eviction silently drops spans with a hardcoded limit and no metric/log
findings.body: `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` trims segments to a hardcoded 1000 spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured value and is no longer used anywhere, so the setting has no effect and the two numbers disagree; (2) the previous code path in `_load_segment_data` that dropped oversized segments emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and `logger.error`, and that observability was removed in this PR. Now span data is discarded with no metric, log, or configuration, making truncated segments undetectable in production.

findings.title: zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting span timestamps/scores
findings.body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. The scores are `end_timestamp_precise` values used to order spans for eviction. If the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a redelivered/duplicated span that landed under a different key before the redirect was established), its score becomes the sum of two ~1.7e9 timestamps, making it the newest member forever and causing `zpopmin` to evict legitimate newer spans instead. The merges should specify `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) to preserve timestamp semantics.

findings.title: `max_segment_spans` is now dead configuration
findings.body: The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere; the effective limit is the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua`. Callers that set this parameter will silently get no behavior change. Either wire the value through to the Lua script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

findings.title: Module docstring still describes Redis sets after the switch to sorted sets
findings.body: The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`) scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted at insert time when a segment exceeds the limit. The docstring (step 3 "Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`" and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes plain sets and says nothing about scoring or eviction, so readers will have the wrong mental model of the key types and of the fact that spans can be dropped.

findings.title: No test for the new insert-time eviction behavior
findings.body: The headline change of this PR is eviction during insert (`zpopmin` once a segment exceeds 1000 spans) plus the set→sorted-set migration, but no test exercises a segment larger than the limit. Existing tests only cover 4-5 span segments, so neither the trimming threshold, the choice of which spans are discarded (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`), nor the removal of the old `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data` is verified. A regression in the Lua arithmetic (e.g. off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`, or the `span_count == 0` fallback) would go unnoticed.

findings.title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new public paginator with non-trivial branching (negative-offset path, prev-cursor extra-row trimming, `enable_advanced_features` flag) and it is already wired into a production endpoint, yet no tests are added for it or for the audit-log endpoint's new `optimized_pagination` code path. The datetime/negative-slice failures in this class would have been caught by a single test.

findings.title: Misleading comment claims a behavior change that was not made
findings.body: The added comment says "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no code changed here — `Cursor` always accepted negative offsets, and callers (e.g. `OffsetPaginator`) are the ones that validate them. The comment implies `Cursor` now intentionally supports negative offsets as a feature, which will mislead future readers into assuming downstream paginators handle them safely (they do not; Django rejects negative slice starts).
